questions.subtopic: 4C2 Dodd-Frank, the PCAOB and Basel. Sharing with a foreign regulator
questions.question: A foreign auditor oversight authority asks the PCAOB for confidential inspection findings on a registered firm it also regulates. Under Section 105(b)(5)(C), added by Dodd-Frank, when may the Board share them?

options.A: At its discretion, if necessary and with the foreign body's assurances
options.B: On request, because Dodd-Frank obliges it to share with foreign bodies
options.C: After SEC approval, because the Board cannot share on its own
options.D: Whenever the foreign body gives confidentiality assurances, as of right

questions.key_concept: Since Dodd-Frank Section 981, the PCAOB may share confidential information with foreign auditor regulators, at its discretion and on set conditions.
questions.pre_read: Read whether the provision creates a power or a duty, and list every condition it sets.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 981 added Section 105(b)(5)(C): the Board may, at its discretion, give confidential information to a foreign auditor oversight authority if it finds sharing necessary for the Act's purposes or investor protection, the foreign body gives confidentiality assurances and describes its information systems and relevant laws, and the Board finds sharing appropriate. The information stays confidential and privileged in the Board's hands.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because Dodd-Frank opened the door to sharing. But the statute says 'may, at the discretion of the Board'; it creates no duty to share.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the SEC oversees the Board. But Section 105(b)(5)(C) leaves sharing to the Board's discretion and sets no SEC approval step.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: assurances are one condition. The Board must also find sharing necessary and appropriate, and receive descriptions of the body's systems and laws.

tips: Eliminate: B turns a discretionary power into a duty, and C adds an SEC approval step the provision does not set.
Final two: A beats D because sharing stays at the Board's discretion and needs its own findings, not only the foreign body's assurances.
Exam cue: 'may, at the discretion of' signals a power with conditions, not a duty; check every condition.

questions.subtopic: 4C3 The Sarbanes-Oxley amendments. Indemnity for recovered pay
questions.question: A listed issuer must recover $200,000 of erroneously awarded incentive pay from its former COO under its Rule 10D-1 policy, and the board proposes to indemnify the COO for that loss. The proposal:

options.A: is allowed if the independent directors approve it
options.B: is allowed because the COO has already left the issuer
options.C: is barred unless the indemnity is disclosed in the proxy
options.D: is barred, as the rule forbids indemnity against recovery

questions.key_concept: Rule 10D-1 forbids an issuer from indemnifying current or former executive officers against recovery of erroneously awarded pay.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the rule leaves any route for the issuer to make the executive whole.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 10D-1(b)(1)(v) prohibits the issuer from indemnifying any executive officer or former executive officer against the loss of erroneously awarded compensation. The recovery duty covers former executive officers too, so the COO's departure changes nothing. Independent directors matter only for the narrow impracticability exceptions, such as recovery costs exceeding the amount; they cannot approve an indemnity.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: independent directors decide the impracticability exceptions. But no approval can authorize indemnifying an executive against recovery; the rule bars it outright.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the COO is gone. But Rule 10D-1 recovery reaches former executive officers, and the indemnity bar covers them too.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because disclosure often cures conflicts. But the indemnity ban has no disclosure exception.

tips: Eliminate: B forgets that recovery reaches former executive officers, and C invents a disclosure exception to the indemnity ban.
Final two: D beats A because Rule 10D-1 bars that indemnity outright; independent directors decide only the impracticability exceptions.
Exam cue: Rule 10D-1 recovery is no-fault, reaches former officers and cannot be undone by an issuer indemnity.

options.C: No; the rule excludes staff of foreign financial regulators
options.D: No; the program pays U.S. citizens and residents alone

questions.key_concept: Rule 21F-8(c)(2) bars awards to staff of foreign governments and foreign financial regulators; citizenship is not the test.
questions.pre_read: Ask who employed the tipster when they learned the facts, and where the SEC's rule adds to the statute.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 21F-8(c)(2) makes ineligible anyone who is, or was when they got the information, a member, officer or employee of a foreign government or a foreign financial regulatory authority. The statute's own list names no foreign regulator, but the SEC's rule extends the bar to them. Nationality is not the test; the examiner's employer is.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the statute's list in 78u-6(c)(2)(A) names no foreign regulator. But Rule 21F-8(c)(2) adds foreign governments and foreign financial regulators, so the examiner is excluded.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because some rules credit internal reports. But reporting to their own regulator cannot cure the examiner's exclusion under Rule 21F-8(c)(2).
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the program is a U.S. one. But a whistleblower is any individual who reports to the SEC; the exclusion here turns on the examiner's employer.

tips: Eliminate: B lets a report to the examiner's own regulator cure an exclusion, and D adds a citizenship test the law does not set.
Final two: C beats A because Rule 21F-8(c)(2) extends the statute's exclusion of regulators' staff to foreign governments and foreign regulators.
Exam cue: for award eligibility, check who employed the tipster when they learned the facts, not where they live.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 The Securities Act and the Exchange Act. What registration does not mean
questions.question: A company's registration statement for its first share offering has become effective, and its investor relations lead wants to tell buyers the SEC has vouched for the shares. Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.A: The SEC has confirmed that the disclosures are accurate and complete
options.B: The SEC requires accurate disclosure, but it does not guarantee it
options.C: The SEC has judged the shares a sound investment for buyers
options.D: Effectiveness shields the company from later claims of false disclosure

questions.key_concept: The Securities Act relies on disclosure: the SEC requires accurate information but does not guarantee it or judge an offering's merits.
questions.pre_read: Ask what registration gives investors, and who is left to judge the investment.
questions.correct_explanation: The SEC calls the Securities Act the 'truth in securities' law: registration gives investors the facts so that they, not the government, judge whether to buy. The SEC requires accurate information but does not guarantee it. Section 23 adds that effectiveness is no finding that the statement is accurate or approval of the shares, and it makes telling buyers otherwise unlawful.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the SEC does require accurate disclosure. But it does not guarantee or confirm accuracy; investors can still recover if disclosure proves inaccurate.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the SEC reviews filings. But the Act relies on disclosure so investors, not the government, judge the merits of buying.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the statement passed SEC review. But buyers keep recovery rights if they prove incomplete or inaccurate disclosure.

tips: Eliminate: C has the SEC judge investment merit, which the disclosure system leaves to investors, and D treats effectiveness as a shield against disclosure claims.
Final two: B beats A because the SEC requires accurate disclosure but does not guarantee it; effectiveness is not a confirmation of accuracy.
Exam cue: the 1933 Act is about disclosure, not merit; the SEC never vouches for an offering.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 The Securities Act and the Exchange Act. A shareholder group's proxy request
questions.question: A shareholder group asks fellow holders of a listed company's registered shares for proxies to elect the group's own director nominees. The group's solicitation is MOST directly governed by:

options.A: the Securities Act of 1933, which governs disclosure to investors
options.B: the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, whoever is asking for the proxies
options.C: state corporate law, since federal proxy rules cover the issuer's own solicitations
options.D: the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, which governs listed companies' boards

questions.key_concept: The 1934 Act governs proxy solicitations for registered securities, whether management or a shareholder group is soliciting.
questions.pre_read: Ask which securities law governs what happens after shares are issued, and whether it matters who is soliciting.
questions.correct_explanation: Exchange Act Section 14(a) makes it unlawful for any person to solicit proxies for a registered security in breach of the SEC's proxy rules, and the SEC says solicitations by management or by shareholder groups must disclose the important facts. So the group solicits under the 1934 Act. Option C is close because state law governs the meeting and the election, but the federal proxy rules govern the solicitation itself.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it concerns disclosure to investors. But the 1933 Act governs offers and sales of securities; proxy solicitations fall under the 1934 Act.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: state law governs the meeting and the vote itself. But Section 14(a) reaches any person soliciting proxies for registered shares, not just the issuer.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because SOX shapes listed companies' governance. But it did not create the proxy rules; they come from the 1934 Act.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the 1933 Act governs offerings rather than shareholder votes, and D, because the proxy rules predate SOX and sit in the 1934 Act.
Final two: B beats C because Section 14(a) reaches any person who solicits proxies for registered shares, dissident holders included.
Exam cue: for any request for proxies on registered shares, look to Exchange Act Section 14(a); who is asking does not change the Act.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 The Securities Act and the Exchange Act. A sales deck in a private placement
questions.question: A company sells new shares to a few institutional investors in a private placement that qualifies under Securities Act Section 4(a)(2), and its CFO's sales deck overstates revenue. Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.A: The exemption covers the whole Act, so no federal fraud claim arises
options.B: The sale breached Section 5, since every securities sale needs registration
options.C: The SEC had to approve the placement's terms before closing
options.D: Registration was not needed, but the antifraud ban still applies

questions.key_concept: A private placement exemption lifts only Securities Act registration; the antifraud provisions still apply to the sale.
questions.pre_read: Separate the duty to register from the duty not to mislead, and ask which one the exemption removes.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 4(a)(2) lifts only Section 5, the registration requirement, for an issuer's transactions not involving a public offering. Section 17(a) still makes it unlawful for any person to defraud or mislead in the offer or sale of any securities, so the overstated deck is exposed. Option A is close but stretches a registration exemption into an exemption from fraud liability.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the placement is exempt from registration. But Section 4 lifts only Section 5; the Section 17(a) antifraud ban reaches any offer or sale of securities.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because many sales must be registered. But Section 4(a)(2) exempts an issuer's transactions not involving a public offering, so Section 5 did not apply.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the SEC oversees offerings. But it does not approve an exempt private placement in advance; the issuer relies on the exemption itself.

tips: Eliminate: B, because Section 4(a)(2) exempts nonpublic issuer sales from Section 5, and C, because exempt placements need no SEC approval.
Final two: D beats A because an exemption lifts registration only; the Section 17(a) antifraud ban still covers any offer or sale.
Exam cue: exempt from registration never means exempt from the fraud rules; check which section the exemption actually lifts.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 The Securities Act and the Exchange Act. Registering a trading business
questions.question: A fintech firm will launch an app that executes customers' stock orders nationwide for a commission per trade. Before launch, the firm itself must FIRST:

options.A: register with the SEC as a broker under the Exchange Act
options.B: register a class of its own shares under Exchange Act Section 12
options.C: file a Securities Act registration statement for the trades
options.D: register with the PCAOB as a firm in the securities industry

questions.key_concept: A firm that executes customers' trades registers as a broker under Exchange Act Section 15(a); Section 12 registers a class of securities.
questions.pre_read: Ask what is being registered: the firm's trading business or a class of securities.
questions.correct_explanation: Exchange Act Section 15(a) makes it unlawful for a broker or dealer to use interstate commerce to effect securities transactions unless registered with the SEC; executing customers' orders for commissions is broker activity. Option B is close because Section 12 registration is also an SEC filing under the 1934 Act, but it registers a class of securities, which makes a company a reporting issuer; it does not license a trading business.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Section 12 registration is made with the SEC under the same Act. But it covers a class of securities, not the business of executing trades for others.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the 1933 Act involves registration. But it registers securities offered for sale, not a firm that executes customers' trades.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because SOX created a registration regime. But PCAOB registration is for public accounting firms, not trading businesses.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the 1933 Act registers offerings, not market firms, and D, because the PCAOB registers audit firms.
Final two: A beats B because Section 15(a) registers the broker's business; Section 12 registers a class of securities.
Exam cue: on registration items, ask what is being registered: an offering (1933 Act), a class of securities (Section 12) or a market firm (Section 15).

questions.subtopic: 4A2 SEC rulemaking. Asking for a rule change
questions.question: The policy director of an investor group that files nothing with the SEC wants a disclosure rule amended. Under Rule 192 of the SEC's Rules of Practice, what may the group do?

options.A: Ask the PCAOB to amend the Commission's rule for it
options.B: Wait for a proposal, since petitions are limited to SEC filers
options.C: File a petition with the Secretary asking for the amendment
options.D: Ask Congress, since a statute is needed to change SEC rules

questions.key_concept: Any person may petition the SEC to issue, amend or repeal a rule (Rule 192; 5 U.S.C. 553(e)).
questions.pre_read: Ask who may start a rule change at the SEC, and whether filer status matters.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 192(a) lets any person who wants a rule issued, amended or repealed file a petition with the Secretary, stating the change sought, their interest and their reasons; the Secretary acknowledges it in writing and refers it for consideration. The Administrative Procedure Act gives every interested person the same right (5 U.S.C. 553(e)). Option B is close, but nothing limits petitions to SEC filers or to rules already proposed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the PCAOB writes rules. But it sets standards for audit firms, and it cannot amend the SEC's own disclosure rules.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a published proposal does invite comments, but a petition needs neither a proposal nor filer status. Rule 192 is open to any person.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because statutes rank above rules. But the SEC can amend its own rules, and anyone may petition it to do so.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the PCAOB cannot amend SEC rules, and D, because the SEC amends its own rules without new legislation.
Final two: C beats B because Rule 192 lets any person petition, with no proposal or filer status needed.
Exam cue: to ask for a new or changed SEC rule, anyone may petition; to react to a proposed rule, anyone may comment.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 SEC rulemaking. An exchange's new listing rule
questions.question: A national securities exchange's board approves a new listing standard on director independence. Under Exchange Act Section 19(b), what must happen before the new standard can take effect?

options.A: It takes effect on the board's vote, as the exchange's own rule
options.B: It takes effect once filed with the SEC, as every change does
options.C: It needs the PCAOB's approval, as it affects listed issuers
options.D: It is filed with the SEC, published for comment and approved

questions.key_concept: Exchanges file proposed rule changes with the SEC, which publishes them for comment; substantive ones take effect only once approved.
questions.pre_read: Ask who supervises an exchange's own rulemaking, and which kinds of change skip approval.
questions.correct_explanation: Exchange Act Section 19(b)(1) requires every self-regulatory organization, exchanges included, to file proposed rule changes with the SEC, which publishes notice and invites written comments; no change takes effect unless the SEC approves it or the subsection otherwise permits. Option B is close because some changes, such as fees or interpretations of an existing rule, take effect on filing, but a substantive new listing standard is not one of them.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the exchange writes its own rules. But as a self-regulatory organization it must file proposed changes with the SEC under Section 19(b).
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: some changes, such as fees, take effect on filing. A substantive new listing standard needs SEC approval after notice and comment.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the PCAOB oversees auditors of listed issuers. But exchange rule changes go to the SEC; the PCAOB has no role in them.

tips: Eliminate: A, because exchanges are self-regulatory organizations that file rule changes with the SEC, and C, because the PCAOB oversees audit firms, not exchanges.
Final two: D beats B because only set kinds of change, such as fees, take effect on filing; a new listing standard waits for SEC approval.
Exam cue: an exchange or FINRA rule change runs through the SEC under Exchange Act Section 19(b): file, publish, comment, approve.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 SEC rulemaking. How a SOX mandate reaches listed companies
questions.question: Section 301 required the SEC to put the Act's audit committee requirements into effect for listed issuers. To do so, the SEC:

options.A: adopted a rule it enforces on each issuer, with no exchange role
options.B: adopted a rule directing exchanges to bar listing noncompliant issuers
options.C: asked the PCAOB to adopt the requirements as auditing standards
options.D: issued staff guidance that each exchange could follow if it chose

questions.key_concept: Section 301 had the SEC carry out the audit committee requirements by a rule directing exchanges to refuse to list noncompliant issuers (Section 10A(m)(1)).
questions.pre_read: Ask which body the Act told the SEC to work through, and what that body controls.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 301 added Exchange Act Section 10A(m)(1): within 270 days, the SEC had to direct the exchanges, by rule, to prohibit listing the securities of any issuer that does not meet the audit committee requirements. The SEC did so in Rule 10A-3, and the exchanges' listing rules then went to the SEC under Exchange Act Section 19(b). Option A is close because the SEC wrote the rule, but the Act enforces it through listing.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the SEC did adopt the rule. But Section 10A(m)(1) has that rule direct the exchanges, which enforce the requirements as listing conditions.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the PCAOB sets standards. But its standards govern audit firms; the audit committee requirements bind listed issuers through listing rules.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because exchanges write their own rules. But Section 10A(m)(1) required a binding SEC rule, so compliance was not optional for the exchanges.

tips: Eliminate: C, because PCAOB standards bind audit firms rather than issuers' boards, and D, because Section 301 required a binding SEC rule, not optional guidance.
Final two: B beats A because Section 10A(m)(1) has the SEC's rule direct the exchanges to refuse listing; the exchanges enforce it.
Exam cue: when a SOX or Dodd-Frank duty is a listing condition, look for an SEC rule that directs the exchanges, such as Rule 10A-3 or Rule 10D-1.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 SEC investigations, disclosure and settlements. Exit pay during an investigation
questions.question: During an SEC investigation of possible securities fraud at a listed company, the board plans a $12 million exit payment to its departing CEO. Under Section 1103, what may the SEC do?

options.A: Ask a federal court to order the payment held in escrow
options.B: Recover it later under the company's Rule 10D-1 clawback policy
options.C: Order the company itself to freeze the payment, without a court
options.D: Ask the PCAOB to block the payment as an audit matter

questions.key_concept: Section 1103 lets the SEC ask a federal court to escrow an issuer's extraordinary payments to insiders during an investigation.
questions.pre_read: Note the timing, an open investigation, and ask who must order the freeze.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 1103 added Exchange Act Section 21C(c)(3): if, during a lawful investigation of possible securities law violations by an issuer or any of its directors, officers, partners, controlling persons, agents or employees, extraordinary payments to any of them look likely, the SEC may petition a federal district court for a temporary order making the issuer escrow them for 45 days. Option C is close, but a court, not the SEC, orders the freeze.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because Rule 10D-1 recovers executive pay. But it recovers incentive pay after a restatement; it does not freeze a planned payment during an investigation.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the SEC can seek a freeze. But Section 1103 has it petition a federal district court, which issues the escrow order.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the PCAOB is an enforcement body. But it oversees audit firms; it has no power over an issuer's payments to executives.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a Rule 10D-1 clawback follows a restatement and works after the fact, and D, because the PCAOB oversees audit firms, not issuer payments.
Final two: A beats C because Section 1103 has the SEC petition a federal district court; the court orders the escrow.
Exam cue: an extraordinary insider payment during an SEC investigation points to Section 1103: a court-ordered escrow for 45 days, extendable to 90.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 SEC investigations, disclosure and settlements. What a Wells submission may hold
questions.question: A CFO's counsel ends a Wells submission with an offer to settle, to save the Commission time. Under Section 2.3 of the SEC Enforcement Manual, what will the staff do?

options.A: Pass the submission and the offer to the Commission together
options.B: Treat the offer as an admission that the CFO broke the law
options.C: Reject it, since offers to settle must be made separately
options.D: Suspend the investigation until the Commission rules on the offer

questions.key_concept: SEC staff reject a Wells submission that contains a settlement offer; offers must be made in a separate document.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a Wells submission is for, and what the staff screens out before anything reaches the Commission.
questions.correct_explanation: The Enforcement Manual (24 Feb 2026 edition) says the staff will reject a Wells submission that contains or discusses a settlement offer; offers of settlement must be made in a separate document. Accepted submissions go to the Commission with the staff's recommendation, and the Commission may use them in any action. Option A is close because accepted submissions do reach the Commission, but one carrying an offer is rejected instead.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: accepted Wells submissions go to the Commission with the staff's recommendation. A submission that contains a settlement offer is rejected and generally not passed on.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a Wells submission may be used in later proceedings. But the Manual's rule here is about form: an offer to settle cannot ride inside the submission.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because settling could end the matter. But a Wells submission argues against charges; it does not pause the case, and offers belong in a separate document.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the issue is where the offer sits, not what it admits, and D, because a Wells submission does not suspend the matter.
Final two: C beats A because the Manual has the staff reject a Wells submission that contains a settlement offer; only accepted ones reach the Commission.
Exam cue: a Wells submission argues the case; a settlement offer travels in its own document.

questions.subtopic: 4B3 White-collar penalty enhancements. Two conspiracy statutes compared
questions.question: Prosecutors weigh which conspiracy statute to charge against a payroll clerk and vendor whose wire fraud plot failed. Comparing Section 371 of title 18 with Section 1349, added by Section 902, which is accurate?

options.A: Both statutes cap the pair's prison term at five years
options.B: Section 371 borrows wire fraud's maximum; Section 1349 caps it at five
options.C: Both statutes borrow wire fraud's maximum for the agreement
options.D: Section 1349 borrows wire fraud's maximum; Section 371 caps it at five

questions.key_concept: Section 902's 18 U.S.C. 1349 ties a fraud conspiracy's maximum to the object offense, unlike the five-year general conspiracy statute.
questions.pre_read: Compare the penalty each statute sets for an agreement that never succeeded.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 902 added 18 U.S.C. 1349: anyone who attempts or conspires to commit a chapter 63 fraud offense, such as wire fraud, is subject to the penalties for that offense. The general conspiracy statute, 18 U.S.C. 371, caps prison at five years for any felony conspiracy. So 1349 ties the pair's maximum to wire fraud's, while 371 would cap it at five. Option B is close but reverses the two statutes.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because five years is the familiar conspiracy cap. But Section 902 added 1349 so that fraud conspiracies carry the target offense's penalty.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: both statutes are in play, but this reverses them: 371 is the five-year general statute, and 1349 borrows the object offense's maximum.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because 1349 borrows. But 371 sets its own five-year cap for any felony conspiracy, whatever the object.

tips: Eliminate: A, because Section 902 added 1349 to lift fraud conspiracies above the five-year cap, and C, because 371 keeps its own five-year cap.
Final two: D beats B because 1349 borrows the target offense's penalty; the five-year cap belongs to 371.
Exam cue: a fraud plot under 18 U.S.C. 1349 is measured by its target offense; 18 U.S.C. 371 is the five-year general statute.

questions.subtopic: 4B3 White-collar penalty enhancements. A private company's pension plan
questions.question: A family-owned trucking company's finance director, acting as its pension plan's administrator, willfully withholds a required plan report. Does the criminal penalty raised by Section 904 apply to them?

options.A: No; Title IX's penalties reach issuers and their officers alone
options.B: Yes; Section 904 amended ERISA, which covers private plans too
options.C: No; ERISA reporting breaches by private plans carry civil fines alone
options.D: Yes, provided the plan holds shares of a listed company

questions.key_concept: Section 904 raised ERISA's criminal penalties, which reach willful reporting violations in private employers' plans as well as listed companies' plans.
questions.pre_read: Ask which statute Section 904 changed, and whom that statute covers.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 904 amended ERISA Section 501 (29 U.S.C. 1131(a)), which punishes any person who willfully violates ERISA's reporting and disclosure rules. ERISA covers benefit plans set up by any employer engaged in commerce, whether or not its shares trade publicly, so the director is exposed. Option A is close because most SOX duties fall on issuers, but Section 904 works through ERISA, not the securities laws.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: most SOX duties bind issuers. But Section 904 amended ERISA, whose criminal penalty reaches any person who willfully breaks its reporting rules.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because ERISA also has civil remedies. But Section 501 makes a willful reporting violation a crime for any plan ERISA covers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because company stock links plans to securities law. But ERISA coverage turns on the employer and the plan, not on listed shares.

tips: Eliminate: C, because ERISA Section 501 makes willful reporting violations a crime, and D, because ERISA coverage does not depend on listed shares.
Final two: B beats A because Section 904 amended ERISA, which reaches private employers' plans; it is not limited to issuers.
Exam cue: before applying a SOX section, check which law it amends; ERISA, title 18 and the Exchange Act each have their own reach.

questions.subtopic: 4B3 White-collar penalty enhancements. A false figure in an annual report
questions.question: A listed company's financial reporting manager, who signs no certification, willfully and knowingly puts a materially false revenue figure into the Form 10-K filed with the SEC. Which provision MOST directly makes this a crime?

options.A: 18 U.S.C. 1520, which punishes failures to keep audit workpapers
options.B: Section 906, which punishes willfully false certifications of periodic reports
options.C: Exchange Act Section 32(a), which punishes false statements in reports
options.D: Section 806, which protects employees who report securities fraud

questions.key_concept: Exchange Act Section 32(a), whose penalties Section 1106 raised, punishes anyone who willfully files materially false statements in required reports.
questions.pre_read: Note who made the false statement and whether that person signed anything, then match the provision.
questions.correct_explanation: Exchange Act Section 32(a) makes it a crime to willfully and knowingly make a statement that is false or misleading as to a material fact in any report required to be filed under the Act, and Section 1106 raised its maximum penalties. The manager's false 10-K figure fits. Option B is close, but Section 906 punishes false certifications by the officers who sign them, and this manager signs none.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because 1520 also came from SOX's record provisions. But it covers auditors who fail to keep workpapers, not false figures in a company's filing.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Section 906 punishes willfully false certifications. But it binds the certifying officers, and this manager signs no certification.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fraud is involved. But Section 806 protects employees who report fraud; it does not punish those who commit it.

tips: Eliminate: A, because 1520 binds auditors keeping workpapers, and D, because Section 806 protects whistleblowers rather than punishing false filings.
Final two: C beats B because Section 32(a) reaches anyone who willfully files a false statement; Section 906 reaches only certifying officers.
Exam cue: a false statement in a filed report by someone who signs no certification points to Exchange Act Section 32(a), raised by Section 1106.

questions.subtopic: 4B3 White-collar penalty enhancements. Fine for a firm
questions.question: A broker-dealer firm is convicted of willfully violating the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. Since Section 1106 raised the Act's criminal penalties, what is the maximum fine the Act itself sets for the firm?

options.A: Up to $25 million
options.B: Up to $5 million
options.C: Up to $2.5 million
options.D: Up to $1 million

questions.key_concept: Since Section 1106, a willful Exchange Act violation can bring an entity a fine of up to $25 million.
questions.pre_read: Check whether the defendant is an individual or a firm before choosing a fine cap.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 1106 amended Exchange Act Section 32(a). An individual's willful violation now carries a fine of up to $5 million, and when the violator is a person other than a natural person, such as a broker-dealer firm, the fine can reach $25 million, up from $2.5 million before 2002. Option B is close, but $5 million is the cap for individuals, not for entities.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: $5 million is the Section 32(a) fine cap for an individual. A firm, as a person other than a natural person, faces up to $25 million.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because $2.5 million was the entity maximum before 2002. Section 1106 raised it to $25 million.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because $1 million was the individual cap before 2002. Section 1106 raised it to $5 million, and set $25 million for entities.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, the pre-2002 entity and individual caps that Section 1106 replaced.
Final two: A beats B because Section 32(a) sets $25 million for entities; $5 million is the individual maximum.

questions.subtopic: 4C1 Dodd-Frank's aims and new bodies. Who runs a liquidation
questions.question: A bank holding company's general counsel briefs directors on orderly liquidation under Dodd-Frank Title II. If the company were placed into it, Section 204(b) would make its receiver:

options.A: the Federal Reserve Board, which already supervises the holding company
options.B: a bankruptcy trustee, appointed under the Bankruptcy Code
options.C: the SEC, which oversees the company's listed securities
options.D: the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, which insures bank deposits

questions.key_concept: Under Dodd-Frank Title II, the FDIC acts as receiver for a covered financial company placed into orderly liquidation.
questions.pre_read: Separate the body that supervises a company from the body that runs its liquidation.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 204(b) of the Dodd-Frank Act says that once appointed under Title II, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation acts as receiver for the covered financial company, with all the rights and obligations the title sets. Option A is close because the Federal Reserve supervises bank holding companies, but supervising a company is not running its liquidation, and Title II gives that job to the FDIC.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the Federal Reserve supervises bank holding companies. But Section 204(b) gives the receivership to the FDIC, not to the supervisor.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because failing companies usually go through bankruptcy. Title II replaces that path with an FDIC receivership for covered companies.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the SEC oversees listed securities. But it is not the receiver in an orderly liquidation; the FDIC is.

tips: Eliminate: B, because Title II replaces a bankruptcy trustee with a federal receiver, and C, because the SEC regulates securities rather than running liquidations.
Final two: D beats A because Section 204(b) makes the FDIC the receiver; the Federal Reserve's supervisory role does not include it.
Exam cue: a Title II orderly liquidation is an FDIC receivership, not a bankruptcy case and not a supervisor's job.

questions.subtopic: 4C1 Dodd-Frank's aims and new bodies. A bank's seed stake in a fund
questions.question: A bank holding company with $40 billion in assets organizes a hedge fund for trust clients and seeds it with 40 percent of its initial equity. Under Section 619, what must the company do?

options.A: Sell the whole stake at once, as fund stakes are barred
options.B: Cut its stake to 3 percent of the fund within one year
options.C: Keep it while its fund stakes total under 3 percent of capital
options.D: Nothing, as funds for trust clients fall outside Section 619

questions.key_concept: Under Section 619, a bank's seed stake in a fund it organizes must fall to 3 percent of the fund within one year.
questions.pre_read: Find the two separate size limits on a bank's own stake in a fund it organizes.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 619 lets a banking entity organize and offer a fund for its trust or advisory clients and seed it, but within one year of the fund's establishment its stake must fall to no more than 3 percent of the fund's ownership interests, a deadline the Federal Reserve may extend. Separately, all its fund stakes together may not exceed 3 percent of its Tier 1 capital. Option C applies only that second test.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because Section 619 restricts fund stakes. But it lets a bank seed a fund it organizes for clients and keep a small stake.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the aggregate limit of 3 percent of Tier 1 capital does apply. But each seeded stake must also fall to 3 percent of the fund within a year.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the fund serves trust clients. That is a condition for organizing it; the limits on the bank's own stake still apply.

tips: Eliminate: A, because Section 619 allows a small stake in a fund the bank organizes, and D, because client funds still face the stake limits.
Final two: B beats C because each seeded stake must drop to 3 percent of the fund within a year; the Tier 1 test is an extra limit.
Exam cue: a Volcker fund stake must pass two 3 percent tests: per fund after a year, and in total against Tier 1 capital.

questions.subtopic: 4C2 Dodd-Frank, the PCAOB and Basel. How Basel III reaches a U.S. bank
questions.question: A bank's audit committee chair asks whether Basel III binds the bank directly. As the preamble to the 2013 U.S. capital rule explains, Basel III is BEST described as:

options.A: binding on U.S. banks as soon as the Basel Committee publishes it
options.B: a binding treaty that the Basel Committee enforces on banks
options.C: a Basel Committee framework that binds once regulators adopt it
options.D: a PCAOB auditing standard for the audits of bank capital

questions.key_concept: Basel III is a Basel Committee capital framework that U.S. banking agencies put into effect through their own rules.
questions.pre_read: Ask who wrote Basel III and what had to happen before it bound a U.S. bank.
questions.correct_explanation: The agencies' 2013 final rule says their proposals reflected agreements of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision in Basel III, a 2010 framework to raise the quality and quantity of bank capital. The agencies then adopted those standards, with changes, as their own capital rules after notice and comment, such as the Federal Reserve's Regulation Q (12 CFR part 217). Option B is close but skips that step.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the Basel Committee sets the standard. But it has no legal power over banks; Basel III binds U.S. banks only through the agencies' rules.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Basel III is an international agreement. But it bound U.S. banks only once the agencies adopted it, with changes, in their own capital rules.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because auditors review bank financial statements. But Basel III sets bank capital standards; it is not an auditing standard.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the Basel Committee cannot bind banks by publishing a standard, and D, because Basel III sets bank capital, not audit procedures.
Final two: C beats B because Basel III reaches U.S. banks only through the agencies' own capital rules, adopted after notice and comment.
Exam cue: Basel is an international standard; U.S. banks follow it through U.S. rules such as Regulation Q.

questions.subtopic: 4C2 Dodd-Frank, the PCAOB and Basel. A thin capital buffer
questions.question: A state member bank's CFO sees that it meets every minimum capital ratio, but its capital conservation buffer has fallen below 2.5 percent. What does 12 CFR 217.11 MOST directly require?

options.A: Limit its distributions and discretionary bonuses to a payout cap
options.B: Nothing, because it still meets every minimum capital ratio
options.C: Hand the bank to a receiver until the buffer is rebuilt
options.D: Stop making new loans until the buffer is back above 2.5 percent

questions.key_concept: Under the Basel III-based U.S. rule, a bank inside its capital conservation buffer faces limits on distributions and discretionary bonuses.
questions.pre_read: Separate the minimum ratios from the buffer above them, and recall what each one triggers.
questions.correct_explanation: Under 12 CFR 217.11, a bank whose capital conservation buffer is not above 2.5 percent may not make distributions, such as dividends, or discretionary bonus payments beyond its maximum payout amount, a share of recent retained income that shrinks as the buffer shrinks. The 2013 rule took the buffer from Basel III. Option B is close because no minimum is breached, but the buffer sits above the minimums and has its own consequence.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the bank meets the 217.10 minimums. But the buffer sits above them, and a buffer at or below 2.5 percent caps payouts under 217.11.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because capital shortfalls sound grave. But a thin buffer limits payouts; it does not hand the bank to a receiver.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because capital supports lending. But Section 217.11 restricts distributions and discretionary bonuses, not new loans.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a thin buffer triggers payout limits rather than receivership, and D, because the rule restricts distributions, not lending.
Final two: A beats B because the buffer sits above the minimums; falling into it limits dividends and discretionary bonuses.
Exam cue: Basel III capital comes in layers: breach a minimum and the bank fails the rule; dip into the buffer and payouts are capped.

questions.subtopic: 4C3 The Sarbanes-Oxley amendments. What the smaller-issuer study found
questions.question: In its April 2011 study required by Dodd-Frank Section 989G(b), the SEC's staff recommended that accelerated filers with $75 million to $250 million of public float:

options.A: be allowed to opt out of 404(b) by telling investors
options.B: stop including management's 404(a) report as well
options.C: replace the auditor attestation with a review by the SEC's staff
options.D: keep the 404(b) auditor attestation, with no new exemption

questions.key_concept: The SEC staff's 2011 study under Section 989G(b) recommended keeping 404(b) for accelerated filers, with no new exemption.
questions.pre_read: Remember that a study section orders a report, then recall what that report concluded.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 989G(b) ordered an SEC study of easing 404(b) for companies with $75 million to $250 million in market capitalization. The staff's April 2011 study recommended keeping 404(b) for accelerated filers, with no new exemptions, and rejected an opt-out as too close to a full exemption. The study changed no duty; the SEC later amended Rule 12b-2 so a smaller reporting company with under $100 million of revenue is not an accelerated filer.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the staff did weigh an opt-out with disclosure to investors. It rejected it as too close to a full exemption, given the value of auditor involvement.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the study concerned smaller companies. But it addressed only the auditor attestation in 404(b); management's 404(a) report was never in question.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the SEC reviews filings. But the SEC does not attest to internal control; the study kept the independent auditor's role.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the study concerned 404(b) only, and C, because the SEC reviews filings but never attests to a company's controls.
Final two: D beats A because the staff recommended no new exemptions and rejected an opt-out as too close to one.
Exam cue: a study section changes no duty by itself; check what the study recommended and whether any later rule changed the law.

questions.subtopic: 4C3 The Sarbanes-Oxley amendments. When recovery costs too much
questions.question: A listed issuer's compensation committee, all independent directors, finds that recovering $8,000 of erroneously awarded pay from a former officer would cost $40,000 in outside legal fees. Under Rule 10D-1, may it forgo recovery?

options.A: No; once a restatement occurs, Rule 10D-1 allows no exception
options.B: Yes, after a reasonable attempt, documented for the exchange
options.C: Yes, at once, because the costs exceed the amount to be recovered
options.D: Yes, if the former officer had no part in the accounting error

questions.key_concept: A Rule 10D-1 recovery may be dropped as too costly only after a reasonable, documented attempt, with the record given to the exchange.
questions.pre_read: List the conditions in the cost exception, then check which option meets all of them.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 10D-1(b)(1)(iv)(A) lets the independent compensation committee find recovery impracticable when the direct cost of paying a third party to enforce it would exceed the amount to be recovered. But first the issuer must make a reasonable attempt to recover, document that attempt and give the documentation to the exchange. Option C is close but skips that attempt.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because recovery is otherwise mandatory. But the rule lists narrow impracticability exceptions, including enforcement costs above the amount.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: costs above the amount can justify stopping. But the issuer must first make a reasonable attempt to recover and give the exchange its documentation.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the officer may be blameless. But the impracticability exceptions turn on cost, home-country law or retirement plan rules, not on the officer's role.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the rule lists impracticability exceptions, and D, because those exceptions turn on cost, foreign law or plan rules, not on the officer's role.
Final two: B beats C because the cost exception needs a reasonable, documented recovery attempt first, with the record given to the exchange.
Exam cue: under Rule 10D-1, 'too costly to recover' works only after the issuer has tried, documented it and told the exchange.

questions.subtopic: 4C2 Dodd-Frank, the PCAOB and Basel. After leaving the audit firm
questions.question: An audit manager who left a registered firm two years ago for an industry job is found to have broken PCAOB standards on an issuer audit before leaving. Under Section 2(a)(9)(C), the Board:

options.A: has lost authority, as they no longer work at a registered firm
options.B: may discipline them for conduct in their new industry job too
options.C: may discipline them for conduct while they were associated
options.D: must refer the matter to the SEC, which handles former auditors

questions.key_concept: Since Dodd-Frank Section 929F, the PCAOB may investigate and discipline formerly associated persons for conduct while associated.
questions.pre_read: Ask when the conduct happened, not where the person works now.
questions.correct_explanation: Dodd-Frank Section 929F added Section 2(a)(9)(C): for the Board's investigation and discipline powers, associated persons include those formerly associated with a public accounting firm. The Board may sanction a former associate only for conduct while associated, or for refusing to cooperate in an investigation of that period. So leaving the firm does not end the Board's reach, but that reach stops at the industry job.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the manager has left. But Section 2(a)(9)(C), added by Dodd-Frank, keeps former associates within the Board's reach for conduct while associated.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the Board can reach former associates. But only for conduct while associated, or non-cooperation about that period, not for an industry job.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the SEC oversees the Board. But the Board itself may investigate and discipline former associates; no referral is required.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the Board's reach covers only conduct while associated, and D, because the Board disciplines former associates itself.
Final two: C beats A because Section 2(a)(9)(C) brings former associates within the Board's powers for conduct while associated.
Exam cue: leaving an audit firm does not end PCAOB exposure for past audit work, but new conduct outside the profession is beyond the Board.

questions.subtopic: 4C2 Dodd-Frank, the PCAOB and Basel. A broker-dealer's PCAOB fee
questions.question: A broker-dealer's CFO asks how the firm's share of the PCAOB's annual accounting support fee is set. Under Section 109(h), added by Dodd-Frank, how is it allocated?

options.A: In proportion to the firm's net capital, under Board rules
options.B: As a flat fee charged equally to every broker-dealer
options.C: In proportion to the customer assets the firm holds in custody
options.D: In proportion to the audit fees it pays its own auditor

questions.key_concept: Since Dodd-Frank, brokers and dealers pay a share of the PCAOB's support fee in proportion to their net capital.
questions.pre_read: Recall which measure of a broker-dealer's size the statute picked for its PCAOB fee.
questions.correct_explanation: Dodd-Frank Section 982 added Section 109(h): each broker or dealer pays the accounting support fee allocated to it, and its share is in proportion to its net capital compared with the total net capital of all brokers and dealers, under rules the Board issues. Option C is close because customer assets also reflect a broker's size, but the statute uses net capital.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a flat fee is simple. But Section 109(h) makes each share proportional, so firms with more net capital pay more.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: customer assets also reflect a broker's size. But Section 109(h) allocates the fee by net capital, compared with all brokers and dealers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because brokers pay their own auditors. But the support fee is the broker-dealer's own charge, measured by its net capital, not by audit fees.

tips: Eliminate: B, because Section 109(h) allocates shares proportionally, and D, because the fee follows the broker-dealer's own finances, not its audit bill.
Final two: A beats C because Section 109(h) names net capital as the measure; customer assets play no part.
Exam cue: since Dodd-Frank, brokers and dealers help fund the PCAOB, and their shares follow net capital.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 The Securities Act and the Exchange Act. An outside investor's growing stake
questions.question: A pension fund buys 7 percent of a listed company's registered common shares in market trades and has no board seat. Which requirement MOST directly makes it disclose its stake to the SEC?

options.A: The 1933 Act's registration disclosure for sales of securities
options.B: The 1934 Act's insider reports under Section 16(a), as Section 403 amended
options.C: The 1934 Act's reports by holders above 5 percent of a class
options.D: No requirement, since market purchases are not a tender offer

questions.key_concept: Anyone who acquires more than 5 percent of a registered class of equity securities must file a disclosure statement under the 1934 Act.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the fund is issuing securities, acting as an insider, or simply building a large outside stake.
questions.correct_explanation: Exchange Act Section 13(d) requires any person who acquires beneficial ownership of more than 5 percent of a registered class of equity securities to file a statement with the SEC, whether the shares came from market purchases or a tender offer; a pension plan may use the shorter Schedule 13G under Rule 13d-1(b). Option B is close, but Section 16(a) reports are for directors, officers and larger holders.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the 1933 Act is about disclosure. But it governs offers and sales of securities, not reports by investors building a stake.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Section 16(a), as Section 403 amended it, is also a 1934 Act report. But it covers directors, officers and holders above 10 percent, not this fund.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tender offers draw the most attention. But the 1934 Act's stake disclosure also covers shares bought directly in the market.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the 1933 Act governs offerings, not investors' stakes, and D, because the 1934 Act's stake disclosure covers market purchases as well as tender offers.
Final two: C beats B because a holder above 5 percent files under Exchange Act Section 13(d); Section 16(a) reaches insiders, which this fund is not.
Exam cue: a large outside stake points to 1934 Act stake disclosure; insider trade reports under Section 16(a) are for directors, officers and bigger holders.

questions.question: A controller relies on a published SEC FAQ on management's ICFR report. According to the FAQ's own opening note, which statement BEST describes its answers?

options.B: Commission interpretive guidance with the standing of Release No. 33-8810
options.C: Final rules adopted after notice and comment, binding on filers
options.D: PCAOB guidance that independent auditors must follow in audits

questions.pre_read: Sort the sources by who issues them: the Commission, its staff or the PCAOB.
questions.correct_explanation: The FAQ opens by saying its answers represent the views of the staffs of the Office of the Chief Accountant and the Division of Corporation Finance. They are not rules, regulations or statements of the Commission, which has neither approved nor disapproved them. Option B is close, but Release No. 33-8810 is the Commission's own interpretive guidance, which the FAQ's note describes separately.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Release No. 33-8810 is interpretive guidance on the same subject. But the Commission issued it; the FAQ answers are staff views the Commission has not approved.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the FAQ explains binding rules. But its answers are the staff's own views; the Commission has neither approved nor adopted them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because auditors read it too. But the SEC's staff wrote it; the PCAOB issues its own standards and guidance.

tips: Eliminate: C, because staff FAQ answers are not rules and bind no one, and D, because the FAQ comes from SEC staff, not from the PCAOB.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 SEC investigations, disclosure and settlements. When a settlement becomes final
questions.question: A CFO's offer to settle an SEC matter has the Enforcement Division's backing. Under Rule 240 of the SEC's Rules of Practice, the settlement becomes final:

options.A: once the Enforcement Division accepts it in writing
options.B: once counsel files the signed offer with a hearing officer
options.C: once a hearing officer approves it in an initial decision
options.D: once the Commission itself issues its findings and an order

questions.key_concept: An SEC settlement is final only when the Commission accepts the offer by issuing findings and an order; staff can only recommend.
questions.pre_read: Separate who negotiates and recommends a settlement from who has the power to accept it.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 240(c)(7) says final acceptance of an offer of settlement occurs only when the Commission issues findings and an order. The interested division presents the offer to the Commission with its recommendation, and its support does not bind the Commission. Option A is close because the division negotiates and recommends the terms, yet only the Commission can accept them.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the Enforcement Division negotiates the offer and recommends it. But under Rule 240(c)(7) acceptance is final only on the Commission's findings and order.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because submitting the offer starts the process. But the offer goes to the interested division, signed by the person rather than counsel, and submitting it settles nothing.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because hearing officers decide contested cases. But an offer of settlement waives the initial decision, and only the Commission's order makes it final.

tips: Eliminate: B, because submitting an offer starts the review rather than ending it, and C, because an offer of settlement waives the hearing officer's initial decision.
Final two: D beats A because the Enforcement Division only recommends; Rule 240(c)(7) makes acceptance final only on the Commission's findings and order.
Exam cue: in SEC matters, staff investigate and recommend, while the Commission decides, whether the question is bringing a case or accepting a settlement.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 SEC investigations, disclosure and settlements. Repeating a proceeding in quarterly reports
questions.question: A company's legal team first reported an SEC action in its second-quarter Form 10-Q, and nothing changed in the third quarter. Under the instruction to Part II, Item 1, must the third-quarter 10-Q repeat it?

options.A: Yes; every 10-Q repeats each pending proceeding until it ends
options.B: No; later 10-Qs report it only after a material development
options.C: No; once reported, it need not appear in any later filing
options.D: Yes, unless SEC staff agree in writing to leave it out

questions.key_concept: A 10-Q reports a legal proceeding in the quarter it first becomes reportable and again only in quarters with material developments.
questions.pre_read: Read the form's instruction on when a proceeding must be repeated, not only on when it is first reported.
questions.correct_explanation: Form 10-Q's instruction to Part II, Item 1 says a legal proceeding need only be reported in the 10-Q for the quarter in which it first became a reportable event and in later quarters in which there have been material developments. With no change in the third quarter, no repeat is needed. Option A is close, but the form does not ask for a repeat every quarter.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: pending cases can feel like they belong in every report. But the instruction limits repeats to quarters with material developments.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because quarterly repeats are limited. But a later 10-Q must report any material development, and the proceeding does not drop out of every filing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because SEC staff review filings. But the form's own instruction sets when a repeat is due; no staff consent is involved.

tips: Eliminate: C, because later filings must still report material developments, and D, because the form's instruction, not staff consent, sets when a repeat is due.
Final two: B beats A because the instruction requires a repeat only in quarters with material developments, not in every 10-Q.
Exam cue: for legal proceedings in a 10-Q, report in the first reportable quarter, then again only when something material changes.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 SEC investigations, disclosure and settlements. A witness who ignores a subpoena
questions.question: In a formal investigation, a former controller ignores an SEC subpoena to testify. Under Exchange Act Section 21(c), the Commission may:

options.A: ask a federal court to order the controller to testify
options.B: hold the controller in contempt itself and impose daily fines
options.C: treat the refusal as an admission and enter an order
options.D: ask the PCAOB to compel testimony under its own rules

questions.key_concept: The SEC enforces a defied subpoena through a federal court, which can order compliance and punish disobedience as contempt.
questions.pre_read: Ask which body issues the subpoena and which body can force compliance with it.
questions.correct_explanation: Exchange Act Section 21(c) says that when a person refuses to obey an SEC subpoena, the Commission may invoke the aid of a federal court, which may order the person to appear and testify; failing to obey that court order may be punished as contempt. Option B is close, but contempt power belongs to the court, not to the Commission.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the SEC issued the subpoena, so it seems able to punish defiance. But Section 21(c) gives contempt power to the court that orders compliance.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because silence can look like guilt. But Section 21(c) answers a refused subpoena with a court order, not with an admission or a final order.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the PCAOB also investigates. But it can compel testimony only from registered audit firms and their associated persons; others it can only ask, or seek an SEC subpoena.

tips: Eliminate: C, because refusing a subpoena does not admit the charges, and D, because the PCAOB can compel testimony only from registered audit firms and their associated persons.
Final two: A beats B because Section 21(c) has the Commission ask a federal court for an order; only that court can punish disobedience as contempt.
Exam cue: the SEC issues subpoenas, but a federal court enforces them; look for a court order when a witness refuses.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 SEC rulemaking. A statutory deadline the SEC may shorten
questions.question: A fund's compliance team sees that Exchange Act Section 13(d)(1) still allows ten days to file a large holder's statement. Since Dodd-Frank Section 929R, who may require filing sooner?

options.A: The exchange that lists the shares, through its listing rules
options.B: Only Congress, by amending the ten days written in the statute
options.C: The SEC, by rule, using the power Section 929R gave it
options.D: The issuer, through its bylaws, for holders of its shares

questions.key_concept: Since Dodd-Frank Section 929R, the SEC may set, by rule, a shorter deadline for Section 13(d) statements than the statute's ten days.
questions.pre_read: Read what the amended statute lets the Commission do, and compare it with the deadline written in the text.
questions.correct_explanation: Dodd-Frank Section 929R amended Exchange Act Section 13(d)(1) so a statement is due within ten days 'or within such shorter time as the Commission may establish by rule'. So the SEC may shorten the deadline without new legislation, and Rule 13d-1(a) now sets a shorter one. Option B describes the law before Dodd-Frank.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because exchanges write listing rules. But Section 13(d)(1) gives the power to shorten the filing deadline to the Commission, not to exchanges.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: before Dodd-Frank, only an amendment to the statute could change the ten days. Section 929R now lets the Commission set a shorter time by rule.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because issuers care who holds their shares. But the deadline comes from the Exchange Act and SEC rules; an issuer's bylaws cannot change it.

tips: Eliminate: A, because listing rules do not set Exchange Act filing deadlines, and D, because an issuer's bylaws cannot change a federal filing duty.
Final two: C beats B because Section 929R added 'or within such shorter time as the Commission may establish by rule' to Section 13(d)(1).
Exam cue: when a statute adds 'or as the Commission may establish by rule', the SEC can tighten the duty without Congress acting again.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 SEC investigations, disclosure and settlements. Helping another's fraud
questions.question: A bank's relationship manager recklessly gave substantial help to an issuer's accounting fraud without knowing of it. In the SEC's civil action, can the manager be liable under Exchange Act Section 20(e) as amended?

options.A: No; aiding and abetting still requires actual knowledge of the fraud
options.B: No; only private investors may sue those who help a fraud
options.C: Yes, but only if the Justice Department brings the case
options.D: Yes; reckless substantial assistance is enough in SEC actions

questions.key_concept: Since Dodd-Frank Section 929O, knowing or reckless substantial assistance to a violation supports aiding and abetting liability in SEC actions.
questions.pre_read: Find the state of mind the stem gives, then check what Dodd-Frank changed in the aiding and abetting standard.
questions.correct_explanation: Dodd-Frank Section 929O inserted 'or recklessly' into Exchange Act Section 20(e). So in an action the SEC brings under Section 21(d), a person who knowingly or recklessly gives substantial assistance to a violation is treated as violating the provision to the same extent as the primary violator. Option A states the standard before Dodd-Frank.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: before Dodd-Frank, Section 20(e) required knowing assistance. Section 929O added 'or recklessly', so actual knowledge is no longer needed in SEC actions.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting, but backwards: Section 20(e) applies to actions brought by the Commission, and it gives private investors no claim against those who aid a fraud.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because aiding a fraud can also be a crime. But Section 20(e) sets a civil standard for the SEC's own actions, with no role for the Justice Department.

tips: Eliminate: B, because Section 20(e) covers actions the Commission brings, and C, because the SEC uses Section 20(e) in its own civil cases without the Justice Department.
Final two: D beats A because Dodd-Frank Section 929O added 'or recklessly', so knowledge is no longer required for aiding and abetting claims in SEC actions.
Exam cue: Dodd-Frank strengthened SEC enforcement; for aiding and abetting in an SEC case, recklessness now suffices.

questions.subtopic: 4B1 Records and securities fraud penalties. A scheme in a private company's shares
questions.question: A sales director defrauds investors in a private startup's shares; the startup has no class registered under Section 12 and files no Section 15(d) reports. Can prosecutors charge it under Section 1348 of title 18?

options.A: Yes; it reaches any security, registered, reporting or neither
options.B: No; its securities prong needs a registered or reporting issuer
options.C: Yes, if the scheme failed, since attempts are punished alike
options.D: No; fraud in a private company's shares is never a federal crime

questions.key_concept: Section 1348's securities prong reaches only issuers registered under Section 12 or required to report under Section 15(d).
questions.pre_read: Check the issuer's status against the securities that Section 1348 names, then ask what other crimes remain.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 1348, created by Section 807, reaches schemes to defraud in connection with commodity futures or options, or with securities of an issuer that has a class registered under Exchange Act Section 12 or must report under Section 15(d). A startup with neither is outside it. Option D goes too far: other federal fraud crimes, such as wire fraud, can still apply.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because securities fraud sounds universal. But Section 1348's securities prong names issuers registered under Section 12 or reporting under Section 15(d).
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because Section 1348 covers attempts. But an attempt is limited to the same securities, and this startup's shares are outside them.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: Section 1348 does not reach these shares. But other federal crimes, such as wire fraud under 18 U.S.C. 1343, can still apply.

tips: Eliminate: A, because Section 1348 names registered or reporting issuers' securities, and C, because covering attempts does not widen which securities count.
Final two: B beats D because only Section 1348 is ruled out; wire or mail fraud can still reach a scheme in a private company's shares.
Exam cue: Section 807's crime turns on the issuer's status, a Section 12 registrant or a Section 15(d) filer, so check that first.

questions.subtopic: 4B1 Records and securities fraud penalties. Whose suit the time limit governs
questions.question: The SEC sues a former CFO for securities fraud years after the violation, and the CFO's lawyer argues that Section 804's time limit bars the civil action. Is the lawyer right?

options.A: No; Section 804's limit applies only to private rights of action
options.B: Yes; Section 804's limit covers every civil securities fraud claim
options.C: No; Section 804's limit applies only to criminal fraud charges
options.D: Yes, unless the SEC first learned of the fraud within the period

questions.key_concept: Section 804's time limit for securities fraud claims governs private rights of action, not enforcement actions the SEC brings.
questions.pre_read: Read who brings the case before applying any time limit to it.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 804 added 28 U.S.C. 1658(b), which sets a time limit for 'a private right of action' involving securities fraud, and Section 804(c) says it created no new private right of action. It does not govern actions the SEC brings; other statutes set the Commission's own limits. Option B is close but stretches a private-suit rule to the SEC.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Section 804 does set a securities fraud limit. But 28 U.S.C. 1658(b) applies to private rights of action, not to suits the Commission brings.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because securities fraud is also a crime. But Section 804 is a civil limit for private claims and says nothing about criminal charges.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because discovery starts one of Section 804's clocks. But that clock runs for private plaintiffs, not for the SEC.

tips: Eliminate: C, because Section 804 governs civil claims, not criminal charges, and D, because its discovery clock runs for private plaintiffs, not the SEC.
Final two: A beats B because 28 U.S.C. 1658(b) limits private rights of action only; an SEC enforcement suit is not one.
Exam cue: Section 804 is about investors suing; when the SEC or prosecutors bring the case, look elsewhere for the time limit.

questions.subtopic: 4B1 Records and securities fraud penalties. Workpapers shredded after five years
questions.question: An audit partner knowingly and willfully shreds an issuer's audit workpapers after the statute's five-year period in Section 1520(a)(1) but within the longer period Rule 2-06 sets. Is that a crime under Section 1520?

options.A: No; the criminal duty ends once the statute's five years have passed
options.B: No; breaking an SEC rule can bring only civil sanctions
options.C: Yes; the penalty also covers willful breaches of the SEC rule
options.D: Yes, but only if an SEC investigation was open at the time

questions.key_concept: Section 1520(b) makes a knowing and willful breach of the SEC's retention rules a crime, as well as a breach of the statute's own period.
questions.pre_read: List everything the statute's penalty clause reaches, then compare the statute's period with the SEC rule's longer one.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 1520(b) punishes knowingly and willfully violating either the five-year duty in subsection (a)(1) or any rule the SEC adopted under subsection (a)(2), with up to 10 years in prison. Rule 2-06 is such a rule, so willfully destroying workpapers inside its longer period is a crime. Option A treats the statute's five years as the only criminal line.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the statute's own retention period is five years. But Section 1520(b) also covers willful violations of the SEC's retention rule, which runs longer.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because SEC rules usually bring civil sanctions. But Section 1520(b) makes a knowing and willful breach of the SEC's retention rules a crime.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because Section 1519 turns on obstructing a federal matter. Section 1520 needs no investigation; it punishes willfully failing to keep workpapers as required.

tips: Eliminate: B, because Section 1520(b) attaches criminal penalties to the SEC's retention rules, and D, because Section 1520 needs no pending investigation.
Final two: C beats A because Section 1520(b) reaches willful breaches of the rules under subsection (a)(2), not just the statute's five years.
Exam cue: under Section 802, the SEC's retention rule carries the statute's criminal penalty, so the longer rule period is the one that counts.

questions.subtopic: 4B2 Whistleblower protection. A hotline report, then a tip
questions.question: An accountant reports a fraud on the company hotline, then gives the SEC the same information on Form TCR 100 days later. For an award, when does Rule 21F-4(b)(7) treat it as provided?

options.A: On the Form TCR date, as internal reports earn no credit
options.B: Never, since reporting inside the company first forfeits it
options.C: On the hotline date, whenever the SEC filing is finally made
options.D: On the hotline date, since the SEC filing came within 120 days

questions.key_concept: Information reported internally first counts as given to the SEC on the internal report date if it reaches the SEC within 120 days.
questions.pre_read: Note both dates in the stem, then check the condition the rule sets for looking back.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 21F-4(b)(7) says that if a person reports to an entity's internal whistleblower, legal or compliance procedures and, within 120 days, submits the same information to the SEC under Rule 21F-9, the SEC treats it as provided on the date of the internal report. The SEC filing came 100 days later, so the hotline date counts. Option C misses the 120-day condition.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the SEC receives the tip later. But Rule 21F-4(b)(7) credits the earlier internal report date when the SEC filing follows within 120 days.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting, but backwards: reporting internally first does not forfeit an award, and Rule 21F-4(b)(7) can even give the tip an earlier date.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the rule does look back to the internal report. But only if the same information reaches the SEC within 120 days of that report.

tips: Eliminate: A, because Rule 21F-4(b)(7) looks back to the internal report, and B, because reporting internally first does not forfeit an award.
Final two: D beats C because the look-back applies only when the SEC submission follows within 120 days of the internal report.
Exam cue: internal report first, then the SEC within 120 days, and the SEC dates the tip from the internal report.

questions.subtopic: 4B2 Whistleblower protection. A consent clause in an exit agreement
questions.question: A listed company's separation agreement bars departing staff from discussing company matters with any government agency without the general counsel's consent. How does Rule 21F-17(a) treat this clause?

options.A: It is valid, as long as the company never retaliates afterward
options.B: It impedes employees from contacting SEC staff about violations
options.C: It matters only once an employee has already reported to the SEC
options.D: It needs the Labor Department's approval before it can be enforced

questions.key_concept: No person may impede anyone from communicating directly with SEC staff about a possible securities law violation, including through confidentiality agreements.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the clause stands between a person and SEC staff, whatever happens afterward.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 21F-17(a) says no person may take any action to impede an individual from communicating directly with SEC staff about a possible securities law violation, including by enforcing or threatening to enforce a confidentiality agreement. A consent requirement for talking to any agency does exactly that. Option C is close, but the rule protects the communication before any tip is made.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because retaliation is a separate wrong. But Rule 21F-17(a) bars impeding contact with SEC staff, whether or not anyone is later punished.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: some protections start only after a person reports to the SEC. Rule 21F-17(a) instead bars any action that impedes the communication in the first place.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because Section 806 complaints go to Labor. But no Labor Department approval can save a clause that impedes contact with SEC staff.

tips: Eliminate: A, because Rule 21F-17(a) bars impeding contact, retaliation or not, and D, because no Labor Department approval applies to such clauses.
Final two: B beats C because Rule 21F-17(a) protects the act of contacting SEC staff, so it applies before any tip is filed.
Exam cue: a confidentiality or consent clause that stands between an employee and SEC staff points to Rule 21F-17(a).
