questions.subtopic: 4B2 Whistleblower protection. A tipster who took part
questions.question: A vice-president who joined but never planned or directed a fraud, and is not criminally charged, gave the SEC original information for a $12 million action. Under Rules 21F-6 and 21F-8, is an award possible?

options.A: Eligible, but their part in the fraud may reduce the award
options.B: Not eligible, since they never reported it inside the company first
options.C: Eligible, and their part in the fraud may not be weighed
options.D: Not eligible, since anyone who took part in a fraud is barred

questions.key_concept: Taking part in the violation does not by itself bar an award; culpability may lower it, and a related criminal conviction bars it.
questions.pre_read: Separate what bars an award outright from what only changes its size.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 21F-6(b)(1) makes culpability, such as a role in the violations, a factor that may decrease an award. Taking part is not a bar in itself: Section 21F(c)(2)(B) bars an award after a related criminal conviction, and there is none. Rule 21F-16 leaves out sanctions tied to conduct the whistleblower directed, planned or initiated, and this vice-president did neither. Option D treats taking part as a bar.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the SEC values internal reporting. But it is not a condition of eligibility; Rule 21F-6 treats it as a factor that can raise an award.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vice-president brought the case to light. But Rule 21F-6(b)(1) makes culpability a factor that may lower the award.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: taking part does count against the vice-president. But it is no bar in itself; Section 21F(c)(2)(B) bars an award after a related criminal conviction.

tips: Eliminate: B, because internal reporting is not a condition of an award, and C, because Rule 21F-6(b)(1) lets culpability lower the award.
Final two: A beats D because, for a culpable tipster, Section 21F(c)(2)(B) bars an award only on a related criminal conviction; Rule 21F-6 weighs involvement short of that as a reduction.
Exam cue: for a culpable tipster, ask about a related criminal conviction: a conviction bars the award, while involvement alone only reduces it.

questions.subtopic: 4B2 Whistleblower protection. Reporting without a name
questions.question: An analyst wants to report an issuer's fraud to the SEC without giving their name and still be eligible for an award. Under Rule 21F-7(b), the analyst must:

options.A: file on the SEC's online portal and leave the name field blank
options.B: report first through the issuer's hotline, which keeps names private
options.C: have an attorney represent them and submit the tip for them
options.D: ask the Department of Labor to forward the tip under seal

questions.key_concept: An anonymous whistleblower who wants an award must be represented by an attorney, who submits the tip, and must reveal their identity before payment.
questions.pre_read: Look for the condition the SEC rules attach to anonymity, not just a way to hide a name.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 21F-7(b) lets a whistleblower submit anonymously only if an attorney represents them for both the submission and the award claim, with the attorney's name given when the tip is submitted under Rule 21F-9's procedures. Before any award is paid, the person must reveal their identity to the SEC. Option A is close, but leaving the name blank alone is not enough.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the online portal is a proper channel. But an anonymous award claimant must act through an attorney, who submits the information on their behalf.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because hotlines can be anonymous. But internal reporting is neither required nor a way to file anonymously with the SEC.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because Section 806 complaints go to Labor. But Dodd-Frank tips go to the SEC, and anonymity there runs through an attorney.

tips: Eliminate: B, because internal reporting is neither required nor a way to file anonymously with the SEC, and D, because SEC tips do not pass through the Labor Department.
Final two: C beats A because Rule 21F-7(b) requires an attorney to represent an anonymous whistleblower and submit the tip for them.

questions.subtopic: 4C1 Dodd-Frank's aims and new bodies. Matching an aim to its body
questions.question: A lender's compliance head maps each Dodd-Frank aim to the body created for it. Under Section 1011, which body regulates the loans, cards and deposit accounts offered to households?

options.A: The Office of the Investor Advocate, set up inside the Commission
options.B: The Federal Insurance Office, set up inside the Treasury
options.C: The Financial Stability Oversight Council, set up by Title I
options.D: The Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection, an independent bureau

questions.key_concept: Dodd-Frank Title X created the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection to regulate consumer financial products and services.
questions.pre_read: Match the aim in the stem to the title of the Act that serves it.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 1011, in Title X, established the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection as an independent bureau in the Federal Reserve System to regulate the offering and provision of consumer financial products or services under the federal consumer financial laws. It serves the Act's stated aim of protecting consumers from abusive financial services practices. Option A is close, but the Investor Advocate helps securities investors from inside the SEC.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Section 915 created the Office of the Investor Advocate to help retail investors. But it sits within the SEC and does not regulate consumer financial products.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is another new Dodd-Frank office. But its field is insurance, and it sits within the Treasury rather than regulating consumer lending.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because Title I created it. But regulating consumer financial products belongs to the Title X bureau, not to the Council.

tips: Eliminate: B, because that office's field is insurance, and C, because the Council is a Title I body, not the consumer regulator.
Final two: D beats A because Section 1011 created the consumer bureau to regulate consumer financial products; the Investor Advocate works inside the SEC for investors.
Exam cue: consumer financial products point to the Title X bureau; securities investors' concerns point to the SEC and its Investor Advocate.

questions.subtopic: 4C1 Dodd-Frank's aims and new bodies. A split vote on a nonbank company
questions.question: The FSOC's ten voting members vote eight to two to put a large asset manager under Federal Reserve supervision, and the Chairperson is one of the two against. Under Section 113, what is the result?

options.A: Designated, since eight of ten votes exceeds two-thirds
options.B: Not designated, since the Chairperson must vote in favor
options.C: Designated, since the Chairperson's no counts only in a tie
options.D: Not designated, since Section 113 requires a unanimous vote

questions.key_concept: An FSOC determination on a nonbank financial company needs two-thirds of the voting members serving, including the Chairperson's affirmative vote.
questions.pre_read: Count the votes, then check whether the rule also names a member whose vote is required.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 113(a)(1) lets the Council subject a U.S. nonbank financial company to Federal Reserve supervision only by a vote of at least two-thirds of the voting members then serving, including an affirmative vote by the Chairperson. Eight of ten clears two-thirds, but the Chairperson voted no, so the determination fails. Option A counts the votes but misses that required yes.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: eight of ten does exceed two-thirds. But Section 113 also requires the Chairperson's affirmative vote, which is missing here.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because chairs often vote only to break ties. But Section 113 makes the Chairperson's affirmative vote part of the required two-thirds, so a no blocks the determination.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because designation is a serious step. But Section 113 needs two-thirds of the voting members serving plus the Chairperson's yes, not unanimity.

tips: Eliminate: C, because Section 113 gives the Chairperson's vote a required role, not a tie-breaking one, and D, because Section 113 sets a two-thirds vote, not unanimity.
Final two: B beats A because the two-thirds count is not enough on its own; Section 113 also requires the Chairperson's affirmative vote.
Exam cue: an FSOC nonbank designation needs two locks: two-thirds of the voting members serving and the Chairperson's yes.

questions.subtopic: 4C1 Dodd-Frank's aims and new bodies. Who recommends a broker's liquidation
questions.question: The Treasury Secretary is weighing orderly liquidation of a failing financial company whose largest U.S. subsidiary is a broker-dealer. Under Dodd-Frank Section 203(a), whose written recommendation is required?

options.A: Two-thirds of the Federal Reserve Board and of the FDIC's board
options.B: The SEC alone, acting as the broker-dealer's primary regulator
options.C: Two-thirds of the Federal Reserve Board and of the SEC's members
options.D: The Federal Reserve Board with the Federal Insurance Office's Director

questions.key_concept: When a broker-dealer is the largest U.S. subsidiary, the SEC and the Federal Reserve Board, each by two-thirds, recommend orderly liquidation.
questions.pre_read: Identify the kind of company in the stem, then match it to the pair of bodies the section names for it.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 203(a)(1)(B) says that when a broker or dealer is the financial company's largest U.S. subsidiary, the SEC and the Federal Reserve Board consider the written recommendation, which needs at least two-thirds of each body's members then serving, in consultation with the FDIC. The Treasury Secretary then makes the determination. Option A is the general pairing for other financial companies.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Federal Reserve and FDIC board votes are the general rule. But Section 203(a)(1)(B) puts the SEC in the FDIC's place when a broker-dealer is the largest subsidiary.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the SEC regulates broker-dealers. But it acts with the Federal Reserve Board, each by a two-thirds vote, not alone.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because Title II pairs the Federal Reserve with another body. But the insurance office director's approval applies when the largest subsidiary is an insurer.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the SEC acts jointly with the Federal Reserve Board, not alone, and D, because the insurance office director's role covers insurers.
Final two: C beats A because Section 203(a)(1)(B) substitutes the SEC for the FDIC's board when the largest U.S. subsidiary is a broker-dealer.
Exam cue: an orderly liquidation starts with two-thirds recommendations: the Federal Reserve plus the FDIC, or the SEC for broker-dealers, or the insurance office for insurers.

questions.subtopic: 4C1 Dodd-Frank's aims and new bodies. Pay of an executive behind a failure
questions.question: An orderly liquidation's receiver finds a former CFO substantially responsible for the company's failure; their last bonus came 18 months before the receiver's appointment. Under Section 210(s), can the receiver recover it?

options.A: Yes; it was paid within the two years before the appointment
options.B: Yes, but only if a restatement shows the bonus was too high
options.C: No, unless the receiver proves the CFO committed fraud
options.D: No; pay an executive already received cannot be recovered

questions.key_concept: The receiver may recover two years of compensation from senior executives substantially responsible for a failure, with no time limit for fraud.
questions.pre_read: Check what triggers the recovery, then check the look-back period and what fraud changes.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 210(s) lets the receiver recover from any current or former senior executive or director substantially responsible for the company's failed condition any compensation received in the two years before the receiver was appointed; for fraud, no time limit applies. The bonus came 18 months before, so it is within reach. Option C misreads fraud as a condition rather than a way past the two years.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because listed companies' recovery policies turn on restatements. But Section 210(s) turns on responsibility for the failure, not on a restatement.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: fraud does matter under Section 210(s). But it only removes the two-year limit; inside two years, substantial responsibility for the failure is enough.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because bonuses usually feel final. But Section 210(s) expressly lets the receiver recover compensation already received by responsible executives.

tips: Eliminate: B, because Section 210(s) does not depend on a restatement, and D, because it expressly reaches compensation already received.
Final two: A beats C because fraud only lifts the two-year limit; within two years, substantial responsibility for the failure is enough.
Exam cue: in an orderly liquidation, the receiver can claw back two years of pay from executives substantially responsible, and more where there was fraud.

questions.subtopic: 4C1 Dodd-Frank's aims and new bodies. Asking an insurer for data
questions.question: The Federal Insurance Office wants claims data from a large property insurer. Before requiring the insurer to submit it under Dodd-Frank, what must the Office do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the FSOC to designate the insurer for Federal Reserve supervision
options.B: Issue a subpoena, since the Office cannot ask for data directly
options.C: Get the state regulator's consent to examine the insurer on site
options.D: Check if state regulators or other agencies already hold the data

questions.key_concept: Before requiring an insurer's data, the Federal Insurance Office must first check with other regulators and public sources for it.
questions.pre_read: Look for the step the law puts before any demand on the insurer, and keep subpoenas for later.
questions.correct_explanation: 31 U.S.C. 313(e), added by Dodd-Frank Section 502, lets the Office require data from an insurer, but first it must coordinate with each relevant federal agency and state insurance regulator, and check public sources, to see if the data is available in a timely way; if so, it must get the data there. Option B is close, but a subpoena needs a written finding, after that coordination.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the Office may recommend designations. But collecting data from an insurer does not depend on any FSOC designation.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the Office does have subpoena power. But it may subpoena only after a written finding that the data is needed and that it has coordinated with other regulators.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because state regulators examine insurers. But Section 313(e) deals with requests for data, and its first step is checking whether others already hold it.

tips: Eliminate: A, because data collection needs no FSOC designation, and C, because Section 313(e) deals with data requests, not on-site examinations.
Final two: D beats B because the Office must first coordinate with other regulators and public sources; a subpoena needs a written finding after that.
Exam cue: the Federal Insurance Office gathers data, but only after checking whether other regulators or public sources already have it.

questions.subtopic: 4C2 Dodd-Frank, the PCAOB and Basel. Standards for a broker-dealer's annual report
questions.question: A registered broker-dealer's CFO engages the independent auditor to examine its annual financial report. Under Rule 17a-5(g) as now in force, which standards must the independent auditor's examination follow?

options.A: The AICPA's auditing standards for audits of nonpublic companies
options.B: The standards of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board
options.C: The examination rules set by the broker-dealer's own SRO
options.D: International Standards on Auditing, if the broker-dealer chooses

questions.key_concept: A broker-dealer's independent auditor examines its annual financial report under PCAOB standards, whether or not the broker-dealer is a public company.
questions.pre_read: Check what the SEC rule names for the independent auditor's work, not what fits the broker-dealer's ownership.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 17a-5(g) has the broker-dealer engage its independent auditor (the rule says independent public accountant) to examine the annual financial report in accordance with PCAOB standards, and Rule 17a-5(f)(1) requires PCAOB registration where the Sarbanes-Oxley Act requires it. Option A is close because many broker-dealers are not public companies, yet the rule still names PCAOB standards.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: many broker-dealers are not public companies. But Rule 17a-5(g) requires the examination to follow PCAOB standards all the same.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because SROs examine broker-dealers. But they do not set the standards for the independent auditor's examination under Rule 17a-5.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because some audits follow international standards. But Rule 17a-5(g) names PCAOB standards, and the broker-dealer cannot choose others.

tips: Eliminate: C, because SROs examine broker-dealers but do not set the independent auditor's standards, and D, because Rule 17a-5(g) names one set of standards.
Final two: B beats A because Rule 17a-5(g) requires PCAOB standards even when the broker-dealer is not a public company.
Exam cue: broker-dealer annual reports are examined under PCAOB standards, by an independent auditor registered with the PCAOB.

questions.subtopic: 4C2 Dodd-Frank, the PCAOB and Basel. Where a broker audit case can go
questions.question: A PCAOB investigation concerns a registered firm's audit report for a broker-dealer that is a FINRA member. Under Section 105(b)(4)(B), as Dodd-Frank amended it, the Board may refer the investigation:

options.A: to the self-regulatory organization overseeing the broker-dealer
options.B: to a state attorney general, without any direction from the SEC
options.C: to the SEC only, because self-regulatory organizations cannot get referrals
options.D: to the Federal Reserve, as the broker-dealer's capital regulator

questions.key_concept: Since Dodd-Frank, the PCAOB may refer an investigation of a broker-dealer audit report to the self-regulatory organization with jurisdiction over that broker-dealer.
questions.pre_read: List the referral routes the section gives the Board, and note which ones need the SEC's direction.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 105(b)(4)(B) lets the Board refer an investigation to the SEC; to a self-regulatory organization when it concerns an audit report for a broker or dealer under that organization's jurisdiction; to another federal functional regulator for institutions it oversees; and, at the SEC's direction, to federal or state attorneys general. Dodd-Frank Section 982 added the SRO route. Option B skips the SEC's direction.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: state attorneys general can receive Board referrals. But only at the SEC's direction, under clause (iv) of the section.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the SEC oversees the Board. But since Dodd-Frank Section 982, the Board may also refer broker-dealer audit matters to the SRO with jurisdiction.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the Federal Reserve regulates bank capital. But this broker-dealer's audit matter goes to its SRO or to the SEC, not to the Federal Reserve.

tips: Eliminate: C, because Section 982 added referrals to self-regulatory organizations, and D, because the Federal Reserve is not this broker-dealer's regulator.
Final two: A beats B because referrals to state attorneys general need the SEC's direction; the SRO route needs none.
Exam cue: Dodd-Frank tied the PCAOB's broker-dealer work to the SROs that oversee those brokers, such as FINRA.

questions.subtopic: 4C2 Dodd-Frank, the PCAOB and Basel. Credit ratings in the capital rule
questions.question: When U.S. banking agencies built Basel III and parts of Basel II into their 2013 capital rule, Dodd-Frank Section 939A required the rule to:

options.A: adopt the Basel Committee's text word for word as U.S. law
options.B: rely on ratings from SEC-registered credit rating agencies
options.C: keep credit ratings, backed by a second creditworthiness test
options.D: use standards of creditworthiness other than credit ratings

questions.key_concept: Section 939A required agencies to remove reliance on credit ratings from their rules and substitute their own standards of creditworthiness.
questions.pre_read: Read what Section 939A is about before weighing how the capital rule treats Basel.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 939A told each federal agency to review its rules that rely on credit ratings, remove references to or reliance on them, and substitute its own standards of creditworthiness. The 2013 capital rule, which drew on Basel III and on Basel II's standardized approach, set alternative creditworthiness standards in place of credit ratings. Option C is close, but keeping ratings beside a second test still relies on them.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because Basel shaped the rule. But Section 939A deals with credit ratings, not with how Basel text is taken into U.S. rules.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because rating agencies register with the SEC. But Section 939A required agencies to remove reliance on credit ratings, whoever issues them.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the rule does use creditworthiness standards. But Section 939A requires removing reliance on credit ratings, not adding a test beside them.

tips: Eliminate: A, because Section 939A deals with credit ratings, not with adopting Basel text, and B, because it removes reliance on ratings, whoever issues them.
Final two: D beats C because Section 939A requires removing references to and reliance on credit ratings, not keeping them beside another test.
Exam cue: Section 939A means federal rules stop leaning on credit ratings; look for alternative standards of creditworthiness.

questions.subtopic: 4C3 The Sarbanes-Oxley amendments. A study of exempt issuers' restatements
questions.question: Dodd-Frank Section 989I ordered a study of whether issuers exempt from Section 404(b) have more or fewer restatements than issuers that comply. It assigned the study to:

options.A: the SEC's own staff, reporting its results to Congress
options.B: the PCAOB, drawing on its inspections of audit firms
options.C: the Comptroller General, reporting its results to Congress
options.D: the FSOC, as part of its annual report to Congress

questions.key_concept: Dodd-Frank gave the SEC one 404(b) study under Section 989G(b) and the Comptroller General another under Section 989I.
questions.pre_read: Two Dodd-Frank sections ordered 404(b) studies; match the subject in the stem to the right one.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 989I directed the Comptroller General of the United States, who heads the Government Accountability Office, to study the 404(b) exemption's effects, including restatement rates, cost of capital and investor confidence, and to report to Congress within three years. Option A is close because Section 989G(b) gave a different 404(b) study to the SEC.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Section 989G(b) did give a 404(b) study to the SEC. But the Section 989I study of exempt issuers' restatements went to the Comptroller General.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the PCAOB inspects auditors' work. But Section 989I gave the study to the Comptroller General, not to the Board.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the Council reports to Congress each year. But Section 404 studies are outside its Title I duties; Section 989I named the Comptroller General.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the PCAOB oversees audit firms rather than studying the exemption, and D, because Section 404 studies are outside the Council's Title I duties.
Final two: C beats A because Section 989I named the Comptroller General; the SEC's own study came from Section 989G(b).
Exam cue: Dodd-Frank ordered two 404(b) studies: the SEC's under Section 989G(b) and the Comptroller General's under Section 989I.

questions.subtopic: 4C3 The Sarbanes-Oxley amendments. Where the recovery policy appears
questions.question: A listed company's board adopts the recovery policy its exchange requires under Rule 10D-1. Under Item 601(b)(97) of Regulation S-K, what must the company do with the policy?

options.A: Post it on its website instead of filing it
options.B: File it as an exhibit to its annual report with the SEC
options.C: Send it to the independent auditor to attest to its design
options.D: Submit it to SEC staff for approval before it takes effect

questions.key_concept: A listed company files its Rule 10D-1 recovery policy as an exhibit to its annual report.
questions.pre_read: Ask where the SEC's disclosure rules place a governance document required by a listing standard.
questions.correct_explanation: Item 601(b)(97) of Regulation S-K says a registrant with a class of securities listed on a national securities exchange or association during its last completed fiscal year must file, as an exhibit to its annual report, the recovery policy that the listing standards adopted under Rule 10D-1 require. Option A is close, but posting it online does not replace the exhibit.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: companies post many governance documents online. But Item 601(b)(97) requires the recovery policy itself to be filed as an exhibit to the annual report.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because auditors review controls. But no rule asks the independent auditor to attest to the recovery policy; the company files it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because SEC rules drive the policy. But the company files its own policy as an exhibit; SEC staff do not approve it.

tips: Eliminate: C, because no rule asks the independent auditor to attest to the policy, and D, because SEC staff do not approve each company's policy.
Final two: B beats A because Item 601(b)(97) requires the policy to be filed as an exhibit to the annual report, which posting online cannot replace.
Exam cue: a Rule 10D-1 recovery policy shows up as an exhibit to the annual report.
